title: What the 'Digital Natives' Myth Is Costing Our Children
author: EdTech Reframed
summary: Drawing on a decade of ICILS (International Computer and Information Literacy Study) data across more than 130,000 students in 34 countries, EdTech Reframed demonstrates that the 'digital natives' label is empirically unfounded: between 2013 and 2023, student ICT use at school rose 39 percentage points while the ability to critically evaluate digital information fell 11 points. The assumption that young people are already digitally competent has allowed schools to neglect teaching critical evaluation skills, and three-quarters of students cannot name a single way to verify a website's credibility. The article warns that the same mistake is now being replicated with AI literacy, building a new assumption on top of an unresolved one, a pattern that will fail the children who depend most on explicit instruction.
points: A decade of ICILS data from 34 countries shows increased technology use does not produce increased digital competence; use and critical evaluation have moved in opposite directions.
Three-quarters of students cannot name a single way to verify a website's credibility, yet most believe they can judge trustworthiness well.
Critical digital evaluation is domain-dependent: generic critical-thinking instruction produces roughly half the effect size of content-specific instruction.
The 'digital natives' label has created an equity trap, failing children who depend on school to teach evaluation skills the assumption says they already have.
AI literacy risks repeating the error, being layered on top of the unresolved digital-literacy gap by assuming competence rather than teaching it.
quotes: Between 2013 and 2023, across the seven countries with comparable data, the share of students reporting daily ICT use at school rose by 39 percentage points.
The unsubstantiated belief that they belong to a generation of inherently skilled technology users may have fostered unrealistic perceptions of their own digital capabilities.
The teachers are not ahead of the students. They cannot model what they do not know how to use properly
Calling young people digital natives is convenient. It saves money on assessment, on curriculum work, on teacher training and professional development.
The next assumption is taking shape on top of the unresolved one underneath, which means that the attempt to build AI literacy risks failing in the same way
